title: The Poet Sultan Called Qutb
subtitle: Budshah Qutb and the Many Tongues of Kashmir
era: Multilingual literary court of Budshah, c. 1420-1470 CE
region: Srinagar, Naushahr and Kashmir's vernacular sacred landscape
moral: A confident culture lets many voices be heard.

sources.note: Primary account of music, poets, courtly performance and Srivara's own literary role.

sources.citation: G.M.D. Sufi, Kashir; Hasan, Kashmir Under the Sultans
sources.note: Accounts of Budshah's Persian poetry, pen name Qutb and musical patronage.

sources.citation: Mohammed Ishaq Khan, Islamic Heritage of Kashmir
sources.note: Modern discussion of Lal Ded, Sheikh Nooruddin and silences in Brahmin chronicles.

dialogue.text: In a valley scarred by bans and burning, Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin—Budshah, the Great King—takes the pen name Qutb and calls poets, pandits and singers back to his side.
Kashmir in the fifteenth century carries old scars from Sikandar’s harsh years—idols broken, music stilled—yet its mountains still echo with Sanskrit slokas, Persian couplets and folk Kashmiri songs.
Raised after Sikandar, Shahi Khan learns Persian for rule, Sanskrit for memory, and Tibetan from wandering monks. Srivara and later scholars remember a prince who listens across languages.
When he becomes Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin, petitions rise from Kashmiri Pandits and townsfolk alike: restore endowments, relax old bans, let recitations and instruments sound again.
Srivara’s Jaina-Rajatarangini says the Great King called musicians back to court. After years when songs were suspect, Budshah chooses to fill his halls with sound.
Under Zain-ul-Abidin, Srivara notes names like Jamil and Mulla ’Udi—musicians and scholars who perform in a revived Srinagar court, mingling ragas and verses for a listening king.
Budshah is not only a patron. Sufi and Hasan record that he himself writes Persian verse, taking the poetic pen name Qutb. A ruler becomes a poet inside his own court.
By lamplight, Qutb the poet Sultan polishes couplets in elegant Persian. No complete diwan survives in the record, but the memory of his pen name remains in Kashmiri histories.

dialogue.speaker: zain_ul_abidin
dialogue.text: Let Kashmiri memory be heard in all its tongues.
Beyond palaces and chronicles, saints like Lal Ded and Sheikh Nooruddin shape Kashmir’s 14th–15th century soul in Kashmiri verse. Their voices flow in villages more than in royal halls.
Mohammed Ishaq Khan notes that Kashmiri spiritual life is larger than elite texts. Under Zain-ul-Abidin, court records, saintly sayings and folk songs coexist, though not always equally preserved.
Srivara crafts his Jaina-Rajatarangini under Budshah’s gaze, chronicling kings and floods, musicians and scholars. His Sanskrit text becomes one key lens on this poetic Sultan’s time.
Reports remember Budshah as conversant in Persian, Sanskrit and Tibetan. His court at Srinagar and Naushahr becomes a place where different worlds speak to power together.
The past cannot be undone. Broken shrines and lost manuscripts still stand. Yet by opening his court, Budshah tries to weave a new fabric of memory and sound over old wounds.
Under Zain-ul-Abidin, grants to Pandits, support for artisans and patronage of singers rebuild a social world where more people, though not all, find space to speak and perform.
When Budshah’s reign passes, dynasties will change and politics will turn harsh again. Yet the idea of a multilingual, musically alive Kashmir stays tied to his name in memory.
Zain-ul-Abidin as Qutb shows how a confident court can carry many voices at once. In every age, the strength of a culture is tested by how many tongues it lets sing without fear.
